hypothesis: If Arizona climate fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years over the last 500 years, then the 100-year-smoothed ring-width series of Arizona ponderosa pine (yellow pine) will show a dominant, statistically significant spectral peak at about 150 years (140–160 yr). That peak will appear in the composite and in most independent long chronologies.
pass_criterion: Select all Arizona Pinus ponderosa (PIPO) chronologies in the ITRDB that cover at least AD 1400–1900 (the original 500-year span), with a minimum of 5 sites. Detrend each one conservatively (a spline or negative exponential that preserves multi-century variance), then apply a 100-year low-pass smoother. Run multitaper (or Blackman-Tukey) spectral analysis on AD 1400–1900 and test against an AR(1) red-noise null at the 95% level. PASS requires both (a) the composite mean series has its largest spectral peak in the 100–250 yr band at 140–160 yr, significant at p<0.05 against the red-noise null, and (b) at least 60% of the individual site chronologies show their largest peak in the 100–250 yr band at 140–160 yr, with at least half of those peaks individually significant at 95%.
fail_criterion: FAIL if the composite's largest peak in the 100–250 yr band lies outside 140–160 yr, or is not significant at 95% against red noise. FAIL also if fewer than 40% of individual site chronologies have their dominant peak at 140–160 yr. Anything between the pass and fail thresholds is reported as inconclusive and does not support the claim as stated, which says 'regular' and 'almost precisely 150 years'. A peak that is spurious or too weak to distinguish from red noise also counts as a failure. A 500-year record contains only about 3.3 cycles of 150 years, so I will also report the spectral bandwidth and the peak-period uncertainty. A peak whose confidence interval spans well beyond 140–160 yr is treated as not 'almost precisely 150 years'.
interpretation: Thompson relays A. E. Douglass's analysis of Arizona yellow pine (Pinus ponderosa) ring widths, smoothed over 100-year means, as a proxy for climate, mainly moisture. 'Regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years' is read as a statistically significant spectral peak at 150±10 yr in the smoothed ring-width series, replicated across sites. The modern reinterpretation is that ring width is a standardized chronology index in the ITRDB (.rwl raw widths or .crn chronologies). Century smoothing is a 100-yr low-pass filter. Significance is tested against red noise, because tree-ring series are autocorrelated, so a peak that exceeds the noise floor is not merely a feature of the smoothing. The moisture-versus-temperature part of the claim is hedged ('probably') and is not tested here. If a second step were wanted, ring-width series could be compared with PDSI reconstructions. The test applies only to the periodicity and regularity of the ring-width signal in Arizona.

dataset.name: International Tree-Ring Data Bank (ITRDB)
dataset.publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), World Data Service for Paleoclimatology
dataset.why_it_fits: The ITRDB is the public archive of tree-ring measurement (.rwl) and chronology (.crn) files, with metadata for state, species code, latitude, longitude, and first and last year. Filtering on Arizona, species PIPO, and series spanning at least AD 1400–1900 gives independent ponderosa pine ring-width records of the kind Douglass used. Fields used: year, ring-width or standardized index, species, location, start and end year.
